name: Seizure Prediction
title: Seizure Prediction
answer: Seizure prediction covers systems that estimate the probability of an epileptic seizure occurring in the minutes before it happens, which is distinct from seizure detection, where the event is identified after it has begun. The work draws on electroencephalography, sometimes scalp recordings and sometimes intracranial recordings from implanted electrodes, along with clinical history and, in some studies, wearable signals such as heart rate or accelerometry. It sits within neuroinformatics and the wider field of the AI physician, where the aim is a warning that gives a patient or carer time to act. The population is people with drug resistant focal epilepsy, the group most often considered for implanted devices.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Seizure prediction covers systems that estimate the probability of an epileptic seizure occurring in the minutes before it happens, which is distinct from seizure detection, where the event is identified after it has begun. The work draws on electroencephalography, sometimes scalp recordings and sometimes intracranial recordings from implanted electrodes, along with clinical history and, in some studies, wearable signals such as heart rate or accelerometry. It sits within neuroinformatics and the wider field of the AI physician, where the aim is a warning that gives a patient or carer time to act. The population is people with drug resistant focal epilepsy, the group most often considered for implanted devices.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The core input is a continuous signal stream, so the infrastructure is built around time series rather than single images or documents. Scalp EEG is sampled at a few hundred hertz per channel and intracranial EEG at higher rates across many contacts, which produces a large volume of data per patient per day. Processing typically runs on a local gateway or bedside device for filtering and feature extraction, with heavier model training done on GPU servers or in the cloud. Implanted systems must operate under tight power and thermal limits, so inference is usually small and quantised rather than a large network. Storage and review sit in the hospital record, and consumer wearables add a second, noisier channel of data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The classical approach extracts spectral power, line length, phase synchrony and similar features from sliding windows and feeds them to a classifier such as a support vector machine or a random forest. Modern work uses deep networks, including convolutional and recurrent models and, more recently, transformer style architectures, trained on long recordings labelled with seizure onset times. Because seizures are rare, training uses careful windowing and class weighting, and evaluation reports sensitivity, false alarm rate and warning time rather than plain accuracy. Patient specific training is common, since seizure signatures differ between people, and some systems adapt online as new data arrives. Validation is usually retrospective on recorded datasets, with a smaller number of prospective trials in implanted devices.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Prediction outputs are clinical information, so the system falls under medical device rules in most jurisdictions, and the site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages covering this area. Performance claims must be honest about false alarms, because a warning that fires too often is ignored and one that fires too late is useless. Data governance covers continuous neural recordings, which are highly identifying, and consent for secondary use in training. Where a prediction is missed or a warning fails, liability questions arise, and the site currently tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies. Provenance of the training data, the model version and the thresholds in use should be recorded so that a clinical decision can be reconstructed later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Near term work is focused on prospective trials that measure real warning time and false alarm burden in daily life, not just on archived recordings. Wearable and subcutaneous devices are expanding the signal sources, which may allow prediction without scalp electrodes for some patients. Personalisation and continual learning are likely to matter more than larger generic models, since the signal is individual. Regulatory pathways for adaptive software are still being worked out, and that will shape how often a deployed model can be updated. The open question is whether prediction changes outcomes, for example by allowing timely rescue medication, and that is a clinical trial question rather than a modelling one.
